lessons.title: Why Does Our Sukuma Wiki Wilt? Anchoring the Phenomenon and Opening Our Questions

quiz.prompt: Amina moved her sukuma wiki plants from the sunny garden bed to the shade of a mango tree. What did she observe over the next few weeks?
choices: The leaves turned dark green and the plants grew faster than before
The wilting continued and the leaves stayed dark green
The wilting stopped, but the leaves became pale yellowish-green and growth was slow
The plants died within a few days
quiz.rationale: In the narrative, shade stopped the wilting but the leaves gradually turned pale yellowish-green and the plant grew slowly. The question checks what was observed and does not ask for an explanation.
quiz.placement: Predict: photographs of the sukuma wiki and the narrative about Amina, followed by silent individual writing

quiz.prompt: Amina's sukuma wiki leaves were wilted at midday, but by the next morning they were upright again. What does this observation tell us?
choices: The plants died and new plants grew overnight
The leaves can only recover if the plant is moved into shade
The soil became dry overnight and the plants then recovered
The wilting was reversible, so it was not permanent damage to the plant
quiz.rationale: Recovery by the next morning shows that the change was reversible. This is an observation-based inference, and it does not say why the wilting happens.
quiz.placement: Predict: prompt 2 'Why do you think it recovers by the next morning?'

quiz.prompt: A mushroom grows on a log and a maize plant grows in an open Rift Valley farm. Which statement best describes the main difference in how they get their food?
choices: Only the mushroom needs energy to stay alive
The mushroom makes its own food using sunlight, while the maize feeds on dead logs
The maize makes its own food, while the mushroom takes ready-made food from dead matter
Both get their food in exactly the same way, from the soil
quiz.rationale: The class collected the idea that maize makes its own food, while the mushroom depends on other organic matter such as the dead log. Both organisms need energy.
quiz.placement: Observe: maize and mushroom photographs, pair discussion on how each gets its food

quiz.prompt: Which list contains ONLY heterotrophic organisms (organisms that cannot make their own food and must take in ready-made organic food)?
choices: Sukuma wiki, algae, cow
Goat, maize, mushroom
Maize, bread mould, sukuma wiki
Goat, mushroom, bread mould
quiz.rationale: Animals such as goats and fungi such as mushrooms and bread mould are heterotrophs. Maize, sukuma wiki and algae are autotrophs that make their own food.
quiz.placement: Explain: two-column comparison of autotrophic and heterotrophic nutrition

quiz.prompt: Striga (witchweed) attaches to maize and sorghum plants in western Kenya and takes food from them. Which special way of feeding is this?
choices: Insectivorous feeding
Saprophytic feeding
Parasitic feeding
Symbiotic feeding
quiz.rationale: Striga feeds on living host plants, which is parasitic feeding. Saprophytes feed on dead matter, insectivorous plants trap insects, and symbiotic partners (such as legumes and bacteria) both benefit.
quiz.placement: Explain: extra minute on parasitic, saprophytic, symbiotic and insectivorous feeding

quiz.prompt: The class has grouped its questions on the Driving Question Board into four clusters: water and wilting, light and colour, food-making, and what plants take from soil and air. Which question about Amina's sukuma wiki best fits the cluster 'light and colour'?
choices: Why do the leaves droop at midday when the soil is wet?
Why do the leaves turn pale yellowish-green when the plant is kept in the shade?
How do plants make their own food?
What does a plant take in from the soil and the air?
quiz.rationale: The question about leaves turning pale in shade is about light and leaf colour. The other questions belong to the food-making, water and wilting, and soil and air clusters.
quiz.placement: DQB: grouping learners' sticky-note questions into clusters under the driving question

quiz.prompt: At the end of Lesson 1, learners draw 'My Starting Model' of Amina's sukuma wiki plant. What is the purpose of this model?
choices: To give the final correct answer to the driving question
To show only the parts of their thinking that they are sure are correct
To show their current thinking, which they will add to and revise after each lesson
To copy a correct textbook diagram of the plant
quiz.rationale: The starting model records each learner's current ideas before instruction, and it is expected to be incomplete. Learners revise it after each lesson and compare it with their final model in Lesson 10.
quiz.placement: Model: drawing 'My Starting Model - Lesson 1' showing what goes into, happens inside and comes out of the plant

lessons.title: Leaf Structure: The Architecture of a Photosynthetic Machine

quiz.prompt: In a cross-section of a dicot leaf such as mango, which layer is made of tightly packed, column-shaped cells that contain many chloroplasts and is found just below the upper epidermis?
choices: Spongy mesophyll
Xylem
Lower epidermis
Palisade mesophyll
quiz.rationale: Palisade mesophyll cells are long, closely packed and sit just under the upper epidermis, where they hold most of the chloroplasts and capture the most light.
quiz.placement: Step 3: shade and label every distinct layer on the printed outline diagram

quiz.prompt: Why are the cuticle and the upper epidermis of a leaf transparent?
choices: So that sugars can leave the leaf quickly
So that light can pass through to the palisade cells below
So that water can enter the leaf from the air
So that the leaf can lose more water vapour
quiz.rationale: The cuticle and the upper epidermis are transparent so light reaches the chloroplasts in the palisade mesophyll, where photosynthesis happens.
quiz.placement: Jigsaw expert group: epidermis/cuticle function statement

quiz.prompt: A student looks at the lower epidermis of a leaf under the microscope and sees tiny pores, each surrounded by two bean-shaped cells. What are these pores and cells called?
choices: Palisade cells and spongy cells
Air spaces and vascular bundles
Stomata and guard cells
Xylem vessels and phloem tubes
quiz.rationale: Stomata are the pores in the leaf surface, and each is controlled by a pair of guard cells that make it open or close.
quiz.placement: Step 4: locate stomata on the lower epidermis and sketch a stoma with its two guard cells

quiz.prompt: The spongy mesophyll has many air spaces between its loosely arranged cells. What is the main advantage of these air spaces?
choices: They carry water up from the roots
They let carbon dioxide diffuse through the leaf to the photosynthesising cells
They store sugars made during photosynthesis
They stop light from entering the leaf
quiz.rationale: Air spaces provide a continuous route for gases, so carbon dioxide that enters through the stomata can diffuse to the mesophyll cells.
quiz.placement: Jigsaw expert group: spongy mesophyll/air spaces function statement

quiz.prompt: In a leaf's vascular bundle, which tissue carries water and mineral salts up from the roots, and which carries sugars made in the leaf to other parts of the plant?
choices: Phloem carries water and minerals; xylem carries sugars
Xylem carries both water and sugars; phloem carries only minerals
Phloem carries both water and sugars; xylem carries only minerals
Xylem carries water and minerals; phloem carries sugars
quiz.rationale: Xylem supplies water and mineral salts to the leaf, while phloem exports sugars from the leaf to places such as roots and young leaves.
quiz.placement: Jigsaw expert group: vascular bundles function statement

quiz.prompt: Besides carbon dioxide and oxygen, what else moves out through open stomata on a hot, sunny day?
choices: Mineral salts
Liquid sugar
Chlorophyll
Water vapour
quiz.rationale: Water evaporates from the moist mesophyll cells and escapes as water vapour through open stomata. This is why leaves lose water quickly at midday.
quiz.placement: Synthesis question: 'What else moves through an open stoma besides gases?'

quiz.prompt: Kale plants in a garden wilt at midday even though the soil is moist, and they recover by the next morning. Which explanation best uses leaf structure?
choices: The cuticle has become thinner, so light can no longer enter
The palisade cells have stopped photosynthesising permanently and died
Stomata are wide open in strong sun, so water vapour is lost faster than the xylem can supply water, and the cells lose turgor
The soil has run out of water, so the roots cannot take in any more
quiz.rationale: In strong sun the stomata open wide and transpiration is fast. Water leaves faster than the xylem can replace it, so cells lose turgor and the leaf wilts. When the sun weakens, supply catches up and the leaf recovers.
quiz.placement: Revising the Lesson 1 phenomenon model with leaf cross-section, water and water vapour arrows

quiz.prompt: Kale plants moved into the shade of a mango tree stop wilting, but over several weeks their leaves become pale and growth slows. Which explanation fits what you learnt about leaf structure?
choices: The stomata in the shade are blocked, so water cannot leave the leaf
The xylem stops carrying water, so the leaves turn yellow
Less light reaches the palisade cells, so less photosynthesis happens and less food is made
The cuticle gets thicker, so oxygen cannot leave the leaf
quiz.rationale: The palisade mesophyll holds most of the chloroplasts and needs light for photosynthesis. In shade it makes less food, so the plant grows more slowly and looks pale.
quiz.placement: Using structural evidence to explain shade causing pallor and slow growth in the sukuma wiki phenomenon

lessons.title: Raw Materials for Photosynthesis: What Does a Plant Actually Need?

quiz.prompt: A student reads that scientists measure carbon dioxide inside and outside a leaf chamber. Through which part of the leaf does carbon dioxide from the air enter the sukuma wiki leaf for photosynthesis?
choices: The roots and xylem
The chloroplasts
The veins that carry water
The stomata
quiz.rationale: Carbon dioxide from the air enters the leaf through the stomata. Roots and xylem carry water, not carbon dioxide.
quiz.placement: Structured reading handout, paragraph A: Carbon dioxide entering through the stomata

quiz.prompt: Which word equation correctly shows photosynthesis?
choices: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water
Carbon dioxide + chlorophyll → glucose + water
Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (with light energy and chlorophyll)
Water + oxygen → glucose + carbon dioxide
quiz.rationale: Carbon dioxide and water are the reactants. Glucose and oxygen are the products. Light energy and chlorophyll are shown above the arrow. The first option is the reverse of the process.
quiz.placement: Step 2 of guided discussion: building the word equation together

quiz.prompt: Chlorophyll appears above the arrow in the photosynthesis equation, not among the reactants. Which statement about chlorophyll is correct?
choices: It is a raw material that the plant takes in with carbon dioxide
It is absorbed from the soil and used up to make glucose
It is released with oxygen as a product
It is the green pigment that captures light energy and is not used up
quiz.rationale: Chlorophyll is the pigment in the chloroplasts that absorbs light, mainly red and blue. It is not on either side of the equation because it is not used up. Carbon dioxide and water are the substances that are used up.
quiz.placement: Step 1 and 2 of guided discussion: difference between reactants and light energy and chlorophyll

quiz.prompt: The balanced equation for photosynthesis is 6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2. How many oxygen atoms are there on the left-hand side (reactants) of this equation?
quiz.rationale: 6CO2 has 6 × 2 = 12 oxygen atoms and 6H2O has 6 × 1 = 6 oxygen atoms, so there are 18 in total. The right side also has 18: 6 in C6H12O6 and 12 in 6O2.
quiz.placement: Step 3 of guided discussion: building the chemical equation by counting atoms

quiz.prompt: A kale plant in a kitchen garden wilts at midday even though the soil is moist. Which explanation fits what the lesson teaches?
choices: The plant has run out of chlorophyll because of too much sunlight
Strong midday sunlight makes the plant lose water by transpiration faster than the roots can supply it
The soil has no water left, so the plant cannot take any up
Too much carbon dioxide has entered through the stomata and made the leaves limp
quiz.rationale: Peak sunlight increases transpiration, so water is lost faster than it is taken up even when the soil is moist. The plant recovers overnight when the rate of loss falls.
quiz.placement: Application question: which raw materials explain wilting at midday?

quiz.prompt: A kale plant moved under a mango tree stops wilting. After several weeks its leaves become pale yellowish-green and it grows slowly. Which explanation fits best?
choices: Shade makes the stomata open wider, so the leaves lose more water
Shade removes carbon dioxide from the air around the leaves
Shade gives the plant too much water, which washes the green colour out of the leaves
Less light reaches the leaves, so less chlorophyll is made and less glucose is produced
quiz.rationale: Reduced light means less chlorophyll is made over time, which causes pallor. Less light also means less photosynthesis, so less glucose is made and growth is slow.
quiz.placement: Application question: which raw materials explain pallor in shade?

quiz.prompt: A learner draws a model of a kale plant with arrows showing where each photosynthesis input comes from. Which set of labels is correct?
choices: Carbon dioxide from the air through the stomata; water from the soil through roots and xylem; light from the sun onto the leaf; chlorophyll inside the chloroplasts
Carbon dioxide from the soil; water through the stomata; light from the roots; chlorophyll in the xylem
Carbon dioxide from the air through the roots; water through the stomata; light from the soil; chlorophyll in the air spaces
Carbon dioxide from the xylem; water from the air through the leaf surface; light through the roots; chlorophyll outside the plant
quiz.rationale: Carbon dioxide enters through the stomata. Water enters through the roots and moves up the xylem. Light falls on the leaf surface. Chlorophyll is inside the chloroplasts of the palisade mesophyll cells.
quiz.placement: My Photosynthesis Model, Version 1: four arrows for raw materials coming in

lessons.title: Starch Test Practical: Finding Evidence That Chlorophyll and Light Are Both Needed for Photosynthesis

quiz.prompt: A leaf has a white region with no chlorophyll, a green region that was in light, and a green region that was covered with black paper for 48 hours. Before the starch test, which region would you predict to contain starch?
choices: The green region that was in the light and the green region that was covered
Only the green region that was in the light
All three regions, because the whole leaf is alive
Only the white region
quiz.rationale: Starch is made by photosynthesis, which needs both chlorophyll and light. Only the green, illuminated region has both.
quiz.placement: Predict: predicting starch in Zone 1 (white), Zone 2 (green uncovered) and Zone 3 (green covered)

quiz.prompt: A learner predicts that the green region of a leaf kept in the dark for 48 hours will still make starch 'because it is still green'. What is wrong with this reasoning?
choices: Leaves in the dark make more starch than leaves in the light
Chlorophyll is only needed to take in water, not for making food
Green leaves never make starch
Chlorophyll can only work when light is also present, so being green is not enough
quiz.rationale: Having chlorophyll is not the same as chlorophyll working. Photosynthesis needs light energy, so the covered green region cannot make starch.
quiz.placement: Predict: justifying the Zone 3 (green covered region) prediction using the word equation

quiz.prompt: In the starch test, why is the leaf first placed in boiling water for about 2 minutes?
choices: To kill the cells and stop enzyme activity
To turn the iodine solution blue-black
To remove the green colour from the leaf
To make the leaf produce more starch
quiz.rationale: Boiling water kills the leaf cells and stops enzyme activity, so the starch present is fixed. The ethanol step later removes the colour.
quiz.placement: Observe: teacher demonstration of Step 1 (leaf in boiling water)

quiz.prompt: During the starch test, a leaf is placed in a tube of ethanol in a hot water bath. The leaf turns pale and the ethanol turns green. What has happened, and why is the tube kept in a hot water bath and not over a flame?
choices: Iodine has been removed from the leaf; a flame would make the leaf produce starch
Chlorophyll has dissolved into the ethanol; ethanol is flammable and must not be heated directly
Starch has dissolved into the ethanol; the flame would make the ethanol turn green too fast
Water has left the leaf; the ethanol would freeze over a flame
quiz.rationale: Hot ethanol dissolves chlorophyll out of the leaf so the iodine colour can be seen clearly. Ethanol catches fire easily, so it is heated only in a hot water bath.
quiz.placement: Observe: teacher demonstration of Step 2 (hot ethanol water bath, ethanol turns green)

quiz.prompt: After the starch test, iodine solution is added to a decolourised leaf. One region turns blue-black. What does this show?
choices: Light did not reach that region
The region has no starch
Chlorophyll is still present in that region
Starch is present in that region
quiz.rationale: Iodine solution turns blue-black when starch is present. It stays brown or orange-brown when there is no starch.
quiz.placement: Observe: Steps 4-5, flooding the leaf with iodine and recording colour of each zone

quiz.prompt: After the iodine test, the white region (no chlorophyll) of a variegated leaf stayed brown, while the green region that had been in light turned blue-black. What is the correct conclusion?
choices: The white region made starch but stored it elsewhere
The white region turned brown because it had too much starch
Chlorophyll is needed for the leaf to make starch
Light is not needed for starch production
quiz.rationale: Both regions had light, but only the one with chlorophyll made starch. So chlorophyll is required for photosynthesis.
quiz.placement: Explain: working through the white zone in the Zone / Colour after iodine / Conclusion table

quiz.prompt: A green region of a leaf was covered with black paper for 48 hours. After the starch test it stayed brown. The region still had chlorophyll. What does this result show?
choices: Chlorophyll is not needed for starch production
The covered region lost its chlorophyll, so no starch formed
Light is needed for starch production, even when chlorophyll is present
Black paper adds iodine to the leaf
quiz.rationale: The covered region had chlorophyll but no light and made no starch. This shows light is also necessary.
quiz.placement: Explain: working through the covered green zone in the results table

quiz.prompt: Sukuma wiki moved under a mango tree grew slowly and became pale. Which explanation best uses the starch test evidence?
choices: Shade gives the plant too much water, so it cannot make starch
Plants in shade make food only from the soil
Shade removes all chlorophyll at once, so the plant makes extra starch
Less light means less photosynthesis, so less starch and glucose are made for growth
quiz.rationale: The practical showed that without light, starch is not made even when chlorophyll is present. Less light means less food, so slower growth.
quiz.placement: Explain: writing one sentence connecting the practical result to the shaded sukuma wiki

quiz.prompt: A learner wants to write a result for the white region of a leaf. Which statement is the best evidence-based conclusion?
choices: The region had starch but it was hidden by the white colour
The region stayed brown, so it had no starch because it had no chlorophyll to carry out photosynthesis
The region stayed brown because iodine does not work on white leaves
The region turned blue-black because it had no starch
quiz.rationale: A good conclusion states the observation (brown), the inference (no starch) and the reason (no chlorophyll, so no photosynthesis). Blue-black means starch is present, not absent.
quiz.placement: Model: annotating the leaf cross-section diagram with a label for each zone

quiz.prompt: On your annotated leaf diagram, you label a green region that was covered with black paper and gave no starch. What should the label say about why starch is absent?
choices: It had no chlorophyll and no light
It had light but no chlorophyll
It had chlorophyll but received no light
It had no carbon dioxide because it was covered
quiz.rationale: The covered zone was green, so chlorophyll was present. The missing factor was light, which is why no starch formed.
quiz.placement: Model: annotated leaf cross-section diagram, Zone 3 (covered green) exit check

lessons.title: Light-Dependent Reactions: Where the Sun's Energy Enters the Plant

quiz.prompt: In a chloroplast, where do the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis take place?
choices: In the stroma, the fluid around the grana
On the outer double membrane of the chloroplast
In the cell wall next to the chloroplast
On the thylakoid membranes inside the grana
quiz.rationale: Chlorophyll, the photosystems, the electron transport chain and ATP synthase are all built into the thylakoid membranes. The stroma is where the Calvin cycle happens. Stacking the thylakoids into grana gives a large surface area for chlorophyll.
quiz.placement: Teacher shows a labelled chloroplast (outer double membrane, grana made of stacked thylakoids, stroma)

quiz.prompt: An Elodea (water plant) in bright light releases bubbles of oxygen gas. Which statement correctly explains where this oxygen comes from?
choices: It comes from glucose being broken down in the stroma
It comes from water molecules that are split (photolysis) at Photosystem II
It comes from chlorophyll molecules that break apart in the light
It comes from carbon dioxide that is split inside the chloroplast
quiz.rationale: In photolysis, 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ + O₂, so the oxygen comes from water. A chemical that blocks photolysis would stop oxygen release, so the bubbles would fall.
quiz.placement: Q1: where the oxygen on the Elodea data card comes from, and what happens if photolysis is blocked

quiz.prompt: In an Elodea experiment, a lamp 10 cm from the plant gave 34 bubbles per minute. At 40 cm it gave only 8 bubbles per minute. Which explanation fits these results best?
choices: Further from the lamp, less light is absorbed by chlorophyll, so fewer electrons are excited, less water is split and less oxygen is released
Further from the lamp, the plant makes more ATP, which uses up the oxygen
Further from the lamp, the plant has less water, so it cannot make any oxygen
Light intensity does not affect the light-dependent reactions, so the difference must be a mistake in counting
quiz.rationale: Less light means less chlorophyll excitation, less electron flow and less photolysis. That means less O₂ is released, so there are fewer bubbles.
quiz.placement: Re-examining the Elodea data card (lamp at 10 cm = 34, 20 cm = 26, 40 cm = 8 bubbles per minute) with the cause-and-effect chain

quiz.prompt: A kale plant grows in the shade of a mango tree for several weeks. It becomes pale and grows slowly, even though it has enough water and carbon dioxide. What is the best molecular explanation for the slow growth?
choices: Shade makes the plant release too much oxygen, which poisons the chloroplasts
Shade gives the plant extra carbon dioxide, which blocks the electron transport chain
Shade stops the roots from taking in water, so photolysis cannot start
Less light means less chlorophyll excitation, so less ATP and NADPH are made and less food can be built in the next stage
quiz.rationale: Reduced light means less chlorophyll excitation. That gives less ATP and NADPH, which slows the Calvin cycle, so less sugar is made and growth is slow. The question states that water and CO₂ are available.
quiz.placement: Q2: sukuma wiki under the mango shade became pale and grew slowly

quiz.prompt: A kale plant recovers from wilting overnight, when there is no sunlight. Which statement about its energy supply at night is correct?
choices: The light-dependent reactions stop in the dark, and the plant gets energy by breaking down sugars and starch made during the day
The plant stores ATP and NADPH in the leaf all day and uses them at night
The light-dependent reactions run faster at night because the leaf is cooler
The light-dependent reactions carry on at night using ATP stored from the day
quiz.rationale: Light-dependent reactions need light, and ATP and NADPH are used straight away rather than stored. At night the plant gets energy from the sugars and starch it made earlier.
quiz.placement: Q3: the sukuma wiki recovers overnight even without sunlight

quiz.prompt: How is ATP made during the light-dependent reactions?
choices: Light energy directly joins ADP and Pi in the stroma
Oxygen reacts with glucose to form ATP in the thylakoid
H⁺ ions flow back through ATP synthase, and the energy released is used to join ADP and Pi
Electrons enter ATP synthase and are changed into ATP
quiz.rationale: Electrons moving along the ETC release energy that pumps H⁺ ions into the thylakoid. The H⁺ ions then flow back through ATP synthase, which makes ATP from ADP and Pi (photophosphorylation).
quiz.placement: Sequencing the reaction cards on the thylakoid diagram (ETC pumps H⁺; H⁺ flows back through ATP synthase)

quiz.prompt: A learner adds a key to her photosynthesis model to show what the light-dependent stage produces. Which list of OUTPUTS is correct?
choices: Carbon dioxide, ATP and glucose
ATP, NADPH and oxygen
Glucose, starch and carbon dioxide
Water, ADP and NADP⁺
quiz.rationale: The outputs of the light-dependent reactions are ATP, NADPH and O₂. Water, ADP+Pi and NADP⁺ are inputs, and glucose is only made in the next stage (Calvin cycle).
quiz.placement: Adding the key 'INPUTS to this stage / OUTPUTS of this stage' to the cumulative photosynthesis model

lessons.title: Light-Independent Reactions: How the Calvin Cycle Builds Glucose from CO₂

quiz.prompt: In which part of the chloroplast do the light-independent reactions (the Calvin cycle) take place?
choices: In the stroma
In the stomata on the leaf surface
On the thylakoid membrane
In the cell nucleus
quiz.rationale: The Calvin cycle takes place in the fluid-filled stroma. The thylakoid membrane is where the light-dependent reactions happen, and stomata are only the pores that let CO₂ into the leaf.
quiz.placement: Part A — Annotated Diagram Walk (annotating where in the chloroplast the Calvin cycle occurs)

quiz.prompt: In the Calvin cycle, the enzyme RuBisCO fixes carbon dioxide from the air. What does RuBisCO join the CO₂ onto?
choices: ATP, the energy carrier from the light reactions
Glucose, which then splits into two parts
G3P, a 3-carbon molecule
RuBP, a 5-carbon acceptor molecule
quiz.rationale: RuBisCO attaches CO₂ to the 5-carbon acceptor RuBP, which forms two 3-carbon molecules of 3-PGA. G3P and glucose are products made later, not the acceptor.
quiz.placement: Part A — Annotated Diagram Walk (tracing the carbon story in red)

quiz.prompt: In one turn of the Calvin cycle, 6 molecules of G3P are produced. One G3P leaves the cycle to be used to build glucose. How many G3P molecules are used to regenerate RuBP so that the cycle can continue?
quiz.rationale: Of the 6 G3P made, 1 exits to make glucose, so the remaining 6 − 1 = 5 are used to regenerate RuBP.
quiz.placement: Part B — Card-Sort Sequencing ('1 G3P used to build glucose' and '5 G3P used to regenerate RuBP' cards)

quiz.prompt: A group is sequencing the steps of the Calvin cycle. Where do the ATP and NADPH used in the Calvin cycle come from?
choices: They are made by the Calvin cycle itself using CO₂
They are made in the light-dependent reactions and arrive in the stroma
They are made when glucose is broken down at night
They are taken in from the soil with water and minerals
quiz.rationale: The Calvin cycle does not make its own energy carriers. ATP and NADPH are made in the light-dependent reactions and move to the stroma, so this step must come before G3P is produced.
quiz.placement: Part B — Card-Sort Sequencing ('ATP and NADPH from light reactions arrive in stroma' card)

quiz.prompt: What do ATP and NADPH do in the Calvin cycle?
choices: They are the 5-carbon molecules that CO₂ is fixed onto
They split water molecules to release oxygen
They absorb sunlight in the stroma
They provide the energy and hydrogen needed to reduce 3-PGA to G3P
quiz.rationale: ATP supplies energy and NADPH supplies hydrogen to turn 3-PGA into G3P. Splitting water and absorbing light belong to the light-dependent stage, and the 5-carbon acceptor is RuBP.
quiz.placement: Part A — Collaborative Diagram Construction (the 'ATP + NADPH' bridge arrow from Box 1 to Box 2)

quiz.prompt: Amina's sukuma wiki under a mango tree receives only 20% of the sunlight it would get in the open, but it has plenty of CO₂ and water. Which chain of events best explains why it grows slowly?
choices: Less light → less CO₂ enters the leaf → no RuBP is made → the plant wilts
Less light → the thylakoid stops working completely → water cannot reach the leaf → slower growth
Less light → the Calvin cycle makes its own ATP instead → more glucose than usual → slower growth
Less light → less ATP and NADPH → the Calvin cycle slows → less G3P and glucose → slower growth
quiz.rationale: Weaker light means fewer light-dependent reactions, so less ATP and NADPH reach the stroma. The Calvin cycle then makes less G3P and glucose, leaving less energy and fewer carbon skeletons for growth.
quiz.placement: Part B — Think-Pair-Share Explanation (why Amina's shaded sukuma wiki grows slowly)

quiz.prompt: A learner is revising her photosynthesis model by adding a second chamber labelled 'Stroma — Calvin Cycle'. Which drawing is correct?
choices: CO₂ enters the stroma, and ATP and NADPH flow from the thylakoid to the stroma
CO₂ and light both enter the stroma, and the stroma makes ATP and NADPH for the thylakoid
CO₂ enters the stroma, and glucose flows from the stroma into the thylakoid to be turned into ATP
CO₂ enters the thylakoid, and ATP and NADPH flow from the stroma to the thylakoid
quiz.rationale: CO₂ is fixed in the stroma. ATP and NADPH made in the thylakoid move to the stroma to power the Calvin cycle, so the arrows run from thylakoid to stroma.
quiz.placement: Model-building: adding the 'Stroma — Calvin Cycle' chamber with ATP + NADPH arrows from the thylakoid

lessons.title: Factors Affecting the Rate of Photosynthesis — Planning & Carrying Out an Investigation

quiz.prompt: A student sketches a graph with light intensity on the x-axis and rate of photosynthesis on the y-axis. Which sketch best matches what scientists find when light intensity is increased steadily, with other conditions kept suitable?
choices: The rate rises in a straight line forever as light increases
The rate rises, then drops to zero at high light intensity
The rate rises steeply at first, then levels off at a maximum
The rate stays flat at every light intensity
quiz.rationale: At low light intensity, light limits the rate, so the rate rises quickly. At higher intensity another factor such as CO₂ or temperature limits it, so the curve levels off at a maximum.
quiz.placement: Predict: individual prediction sketch-graph of light intensity against rate of photosynthesis

quiz.prompt: In an investigation, an aquatic plant (Elodea) is placed in a beaker of water with sodium bicarbonate dissolved in it. Why is sodium bicarbonate added to the water?
choices: To warm the water so the plant grows faster
To give the plant oxygen to breathe
To supply CO₂ so that CO₂ is not the limiting factor and light can be tested on its own
To make the oxygen bubbles bigger and easier to count
quiz.rationale: Sodium bicarbonate releases CO₂ into the water. This keeps CO₂ plentiful so any change in the bubble rate is due to light intensity alone.
quiz.placement: Part B: data collection - probing question 'Why are we using sodium bicarbonate in the water?'

quiz.prompt: A class uses the formula: relative light intensity = 100 × (10 ÷ distance in cm)². What is the relative light intensity when the lamp is 20 cm from the plant?
quiz.rationale: Relative intensity = 100 × (10 ÷ 20)² = 100 × 0.25 = 25. Doubling the distance from 10 cm to 20 cm cuts the intensity to one quarter, not one half.
quiz.placement: Part B: data collection - Option 2 dataset card (relative intensity = 100 x (10/distance)²)

quiz.prompt: A learner plots her photosynthesis data (rate in bubbles per minute against light intensity). Which way of joining the points is correct for this graph?
choices: Draw a straight horizontal line through the first point
Join only the highest and lowest points with one straight line
Join every point with a ruler in a zigzag, dot to dot
Draw a smooth best-fit curve through the middle of the points to show the trend
quiz.rationale: In biology we draw the trend with a smooth best-fit curve through the middle of the points. We do not join every dot.
quiz.placement: Part C: graph plotting - smooth best-fit curve, not dot-to-dot

quiz.prompt: Which statement correctly describes a limiting factor in photosynthesis?
choices: The factor that stops photosynthesis completely when it changes
The gas that is released as a product of photosynthesis
The factor present at the lowest or most restrictive level, which controls the overall rate
The factor present at the highest level, which makes the rate as fast as possible
quiz.rationale: A limiting factor is the factor in shortest supply, or most restrictive, that controls the overall rate. For example, if rain is enough but there is no fertiliser, fertiliser limits tea growth.
quiz.placement: Explain: teacher introduces the term LIMITING FACTOR after the three graph-analysis questions

quiz.prompt: In a photosynthesis investigation, the lamp was moved closer so that relative light intensity increased from 100 to 400 units. The rate only rose from 34 to 36 bubbles per minute. What is the best explanation?
choices: The plant has stopped photosynthesising because the light is too bright
Light is no longer the limiting factor, so another factor such as CO₂ or temperature is limiting the rate
The extra light has no effect on photosynthesis at any intensity
The learners must have counted the bubbles wrongly
quiz.rationale: Quadrupling the light gave almost no extra photosynthesis, so the curve has levelled off. Something else, such as CO₂ concentration or temperature, is now the limiting factor.
quiz.placement: Explain: graph detective question Q3 - why the curve flattens at high light intensity

quiz.prompt: In an investigation, a lamp 40 cm from a plant gave 8 bubbles per minute. At 20 cm the plant gave 26 bubbles per minute. How many more bubbles per minute were produced at 20 cm than at 40 cm?
quiz.rationale: The difference is 26 − 8 = 18 bubbles per minute. More bubbles mean more oxygen released and a faster rate of photosynthesis with the brighter light.
quiz.placement: Explain: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning frame - citing specific data points from the table

quiz.prompt: Sukuma wiki plants moved under a mango tree grew slowly and turned pale. Using what a rate-against-intensity graph shows, which is the best explanation?
choices: In shade the light intensity is so high that the rate of photosynthesis drops
In shade the plant has reached the flat part of the graph, where light has no effect
In shade the plant gets too much CO₂, which slows photosynthesis
In shade the light intensity is low, so light is the limiting factor and the rate of photosynthesis is low
quiz.rationale: Shade is the low-intensity part of the graph, where the rate is low and light limits it. Less glucose is made, so growth is slow and chlorophyll is poorly made, which gives pale leaves.
quiz.placement: Explain: phenomenon reconnection - using a graph region to explain the pale, slow-growing sukuma wiki

quiz.prompt: Sukuma wiki wilts at midday even though the soil is moist. A photosynthesis model shows light intensity, CO₂, water as an input, and glucose and O₂ as outputs. Which process is still missing that would help explain the wilting?
choices: Respiration releasing energy from glucose at night
Production of more chlorophyll in strong light
Uptake of sodium bicarbonate through the roots
Loss of water vapour from the leaves (transpiration) when the sun is strong
quiz.rationale: Photosynthesis data cannot explain wilting. Water leaves the leaf as vapour through open stomata in strong sunlight, which is transpiration. This is the missing link the class will return to later.
quiz.placement: Model: whole-class close - 'What process involving water is still completely missing?'

lessons.title: Factors Affecting Photosynthesis Rate — Data Analysis & Explain

quiz.prompt: In an experiment at constant light and 25 °C, the relative rate of photosynthesis was 4, 12, 20, 26 and 28 units at CO₂ concentrations of 0.01%, 0.04%, 0.08%, 0.16% and 0.32%. What does the change from 0.16% to 0.32% CO₂ tell you?
choices: The plant has stopped photosynthesising
Enzymes have been denatured by the high CO₂
CO₂ is still the main limiting factor, so the rate will keep rising steeply
CO₂ is no longer the main limiting factor, so another factor such as light or temperature is now limiting
quiz.rationale: The rate rises by only 2 units (26 to 28) when CO₂ doubles, so the graph has levelled off into a plateau. This means CO₂ is no longer in shortest supply and another factor, such as light or temperature, now limits the rate.
quiz.placement: Dataset A: CO₂ concentration vs. relative rate of photosynthesis (plotting and annotating the plateau)

quiz.prompt: At constant light and 0.04% CO₂, a plant's relative rate of photosynthesis is 17 units at 35 °C and 3 units at 45 °C. By how many units did the rate fall between 35 °C and 45 °C?
choices: 20 units
12 units
14 units
10 units
quiz.rationale: The fall is the rate at 35 °C minus the rate at 45 °C: 17 − 3 = 14 units. This sharp decline shows that very high temperature harms the process.
quiz.placement: Dataset B: Temperature vs. relative rate of photosynthesis (reading values from the graph)

quiz.prompt: In a temperature experiment with constant light and 0.04% CO₂, the rate of photosynthesis rises to a peak at about 35 °C and then drops sharply by 45 °C. What is the best explanation for the drop?
choices: The light intensity becomes weaker at high temperatures
The enzymes that control photosynthesis are damaged (denatured) by the high temperature
The CO₂ in the air runs out as the temperature rises
The leaf makes more chlorophyll, which blocks the reactions
quiz.rationale: Photosynthesis depends on enzymes such as RuBisCO. Above the optimum temperature they lose their shape (denature), so the rate falls even though light and CO₂ are unchanged.
quiz.placement: Dataset B: annotating the sharp drop ('enzymes denatured?')

quiz.prompt: A teacher explains a limiting factor using a githeri recipe with plenty of beans but only a little maize. Which statement best defines a limiting factor in photosynthesis?
choices: The factor in shortest supply relative to what the plant needs at that moment, which sets the overall rate
The factor present in the greatest amount, because it controls the plant
The factor that the farmer can change most easily
Light intensity, which is always the limiting factor
quiz.rationale: Like the maize in the githeri, the factor in shortest supply relative to the plant's needs sets the rate. Which factor limits can change as conditions change.
quiz.placement: Step 2: Limiting Factor Mini-Lecture with CER (githeri analogy)

quiz.prompt: A sukuma wiki plant is moved into deep shade under a mango tree. It still has 0.04% CO₂ and a temperature of 25 °C. Which factor is now most likely limiting its rate of photosynthesis?
choices: Light intensity, because the light reactions are short of energy
Carbon dioxide, because 0.04% is a very small amount
Oxygen, because the mango tree uses it
Temperature, because shade is always too cold for enzymes
quiz.rationale: In deep shade, light is in shortest supply, so the light reactions run slowly and the overall rate is low. This helps explain why the shaded kale grew slowly and became pale.
quiz.placement: Step 2: CER discussion, Scenario B (same plant moved into deep shade)

quiz.prompt: Greenhouse tomato farmers in Naivasha pipe extra CO₂ into their polytunnels during the day. Under which condition would adding more CO₂ NOT increase the rate of photosynthesis?
choices: When CO₂ is the factor in shortest supply
When the plants are in full sunlight at a suitable temperature
When light is very low or the temperature is far from the optimum, so one of these is limiting instead
When the greenhouse has a low CO₂ concentration of 0.04%
quiz.rationale: Extra CO₂ only helps when CO₂ is the limiting factor. If light or temperature is limiting, the rate stays low however much CO₂ is added, as the plateau on the CO₂ graph shows.
quiz.placement: Step 3: Agricultural Application (Naivasha greenhouse tomato scenario card)

quiz.prompt: Which pairing of limiting factor and the part of photosynthesis where it mainly acts is correct?
choices: Light acts on the light reactions; CO₂ is used in the Calvin cycle; temperature affects enzyme activity in the stroma
Temperature affects only chlorophyll; CO₂ affects only the stomata
Temperature acts only on the light reactions; light acts only on the Calvin cycle
CO₂ acts on the light reactions; light acts on enzyme activity in the stroma
quiz.rationale: Light drives the light reactions, CO₂ is fixed in the Calvin cycle, and temperature affects the enzymes that work in the stroma. These are the three annotations added in the 'Limiting Factors Layer'.
quiz.placement: Adding the 'Limiting Factors Layer' to the cumulative photosynthesis model

quiz.prompt: A farmer in Kericho grows tea in cool, misty conditions (low temperature, moderate light, normal CO₂). She adds a fertiliser that releases extra CO₂ in the soil. Will this greatly increase her photosynthesis rate?
choices: Yes, because more CO₂ always raises the rate
Only at night, when the stomata are open
No, because low temperature is probably the limiting factor, so extra CO₂ will not help much
Yes, because the extra CO₂ will make the air warmer
quiz.rationale: In cool conditions, enzyme activity is slow, so temperature is the bottleneck. As the temperature graph shows, the rate stays low at low temperatures, and extra CO₂ cannot fix this.
quiz.placement: Exit ticket: Kericho tea farmer (3-2-1 exit ticket)

lessons.title: Mineral Nutrition: What Does the Soil Give the Plant?

quiz.prompt: In a maize field in Nakuru, the older lower leaves are turning uniformly yellow while the younger upper leaves stay green. Which mineral is most likely deficient?
choices: Phosphorus
Iron
Zinc
Nitrogen
quiz.rationale: Nitrogen is mobile in the plant and is moved from old leaves to young ones, so yellowing (chlorosis) shows first on the older leaves. Iron deficiency shows on young leaves, zinc causes white striping, and phosphorus causes purple-tinged leaves.
quiz.placement: CER worksheet: photograph A, nitrogen-deficient maize from Nakuru

quiz.prompt: Spinach grown on an urban farm in Nairobi shows yellowing between the veins, but only on the youngest leaves. The older leaves are still green. Which mineral is most likely deficient?
choices: Magnesium
Nitrogen
Iron
Phosphorus
quiz.rationale: Iron is immobile in the plant, so a shortage appears first on the youngest leaves. Magnesium and nitrogen deficiencies show first on older leaves.
quiz.placement: CER worksheet: photograph E, iron-deficient spinach, and the magnesium vs iron interveinal chlorosis discussion

quiz.prompt: Tea plants in Kericho and spinach in Nairobi both show yellowing between the veins (interveinal chlorosis). In the tea plants it appears on the older leaves first. Why does magnesium deficiency show on older leaves first?
choices: Magnesium is immobile, so it stays in the young leaves
Older leaves are closer to the roots, so they run out of magnesium first
Magnesium is mobile, so the plant moves it from older leaves to young growing leaves
Older leaves receive more sunlight, so they use up magnesium faster
quiz.rationale: Magnesium is mobile in the phloem. When there is too little, the plant transports it from older leaves to young leaves, so the older leaves show the symptoms first.
quiz.placement: CER worksheet: photograph D, magnesium-deficient tea from Kericho, and the old vs young leaves teacher prompt

quiz.prompt: How do mineral ions such as nitrates and magnesium ions from the soil enter a sukuma wiki plant?
choices: They enter through the stem bark and are carried down to the roots
Root hair cells absorb them by osmosis, in the same way as water
Root hair cells absorb them by active transport, which uses energy from respiration
The leaves absorb them through the stomata
quiz.rationale: Mineral ions are dissolved in soil water and are taken up by root hair cells by active transport. This needs energy from respiration, and it is different from osmosis, which only moves water.
quiz.placement: Class discussion: how root hair cells absorb mineral ions by active transport

quiz.prompt: A learner writes: 'A sukuma wiki plant eats minerals from the soil as its food.' Which statement corrects this idea?
choices: Minerals give the plant energy directly, so the plant does not need light
Minerals are needed to build things like chlorophyll and proteins, but the plant's food is glucose made by photosynthesis
Minerals are the main food of the plant, and glucose is only a waste product
Minerals are the plant's food, but only when the plant is growing under shade
quiz.rationale: Minerals are raw materials for making chlorophyll, proteins and other structures. They are not food. The plant's food is glucose, which it makes in photosynthesis.
quiz.placement: 'So What?' paragraph and teacher check for the misconception that plants 'eat minerals'

quiz.prompt: A sukuma wiki plant growing under a mango tree has pale yellowish-green leaves and grows slowly. Which explanation fits best?
choices: The mango tree only causes the problem by blocking carbon dioxide, so minerals are not involved
The shade gives less light for photosynthesis and chlorophyll making, and the mango tree's roots may also take nitrogen from the soil, adding a second problem
The leaves are pale only because the soil under the mango tree has too much water
The shade gives the plant too many minerals, which turns the leaves pale
quiz.rationale: Low light is the main cause of the paleness and slow growth. Competition from the mango roots for nitrogen and other minerals can add a mineral deficiency, which also reduces chlorophyll.
quiz.placement: 'So What?' paragraph: which cause fits the plant under the mango tree best

quiz.prompt: Which pairing of a mineral and the plant part or substance it helps to build or support is correct?
choices: Calcium – the cell wall
Phosphorus – stomatal guard cells
Magnesium – the cell wall
Potassium – chlorophyll
quiz.rationale: Calcium supports the cell wall. Nitrogen and magnesium are needed for chlorophyll, potassium supports guard cells, and phosphorus supports DNA and cell membranes.
quiz.placement: Cumulative model revision: annotation arrows from mineral ions to the plant structures they support

lessons.title: Model Building, Synthesis and DQB Resolution: Putting the Sukuma Wiki Story Together

quiz.prompt: A kale (sukuma wiki) plant in a Nairobi kitchen garden wilts at midday even though the soil is moist, and it recovers the next morning. Which explanation is best?
choices: The soil has run out of water, so the plant dies a little each day.
The roots stop working permanently in hot weather, so the plant cannot take in any water.
The leaves wilt because the plant has used up all its minerals by midday.
In strong midday sun the leaves lose water vapour through the stomata faster than the xylem can supply it, so cells lose turgor pressure and the leaf droops.
quiz.rationale: Strong light and heat increase transpiration through open stomata, so water loss exceeds uptake and turgor falls. At night transpiration slows, water supply catches up and turgor returns, so the plant recovers. Wet soil does not prevent this.
quiz.placement: Predict: annotating the Lesson 1 prediction and filling the THEN WE THOUGHT / NOW WE KNOW columns

quiz.prompt: A leaf has green and white patches (a variegated leaf). After it has been in sunlight, it is boiled in water, soaked in alcohol and tested with iodine solution. Only the green patches turn blue-black. What does this show?
choices: Chlorophyll is needed for photosynthesis, so starch is made only where the leaf is green.
Starch is made in the roots and then moves only into the green parts of the leaf.
Iodine solution only reacts with the colour green.
White patches take in more water than green patches, so starch washes away from them.
quiz.rationale: Blue-black shows starch, which is stored glucose from photosynthesis. The white patches have no chlorophyll, so they cannot photosynthesise and make no starch.
quiz.placement: Station 3: photograph of the iodine-stained variegated leaf (starch test practical)

quiz.prompt: Photosynthesis happens in two stages. What do the light-dependent reactions supply to the light-independent reactions (Calvin cycle) so that carbon dioxide can be turned into glucose?
choices: Glucose and oxygen
Carbon dioxide and water
ATP and NADPH
Chlorophyll and starch
quiz.rationale: The light-dependent reactions use light energy to make ATP and NADPH (and release oxygen). The light-independent reactions use these to fix carbon dioxide into glucose.
quiz.placement: Station 4: two-stage flow diagram of photosynthesis with key molecules labelled

quiz.prompt: A kale plant moved under a mango tree grows slowly. Which explanation of the slow growth is correct?
choices: Low light intensity slows the light-dependent reactions, so less ATP and NADPH are made, less glucose is produced and growth is slow.
Shade removes all carbon dioxide from the air around the plant.
In shade the plant makes too much glucose and cannot use it all.
Shade stops the roots from absorbing water, so the plant cannot make food.
quiz.rationale: Light energy drives the light-dependent reactions. With less light there is less ATP and NADPH, so the light-independent reactions make less glucose and the plant has less food for growth.
quiz.placement: Building the annotated model: explaining the shade pallor and slow growth

quiz.prompt: In an experiment, a plant's rate of photosynthesis rises as light intensity increases, then levels off even when the light is made brighter. What is the best explanation?
choices: The plant no longer needs light for photosynthesis.
Bright light destroys all the chlorophyll at once.
Another factor, such as carbon dioxide concentration or temperature, has become the limiting factor.
The plant has stopped making glucose and has started making only oxygen.
quiz.rationale: When light is no longer the factor in shortest supply, the rate is held back by another limiting factor such as CO2 concentration or temperature. More light then makes no further difference.
quiz.placement: Station 5: graph of photosynthesis rate against light intensity

quiz.prompt: Kale grown in soil that lacks nitrogen has pale yellowish-green leaves and grows slowly. Which explanation is best?
choices: Nitrogen shortage makes the stomata close, which causes wilting rather than pale leaves.
Nitrogen is needed to build chlorophyll and other molecules, so less chlorophyll is made, less light is absorbed, photosynthesis slows and growth is poor.
Nitrogen is the main energy source that the plant burns directly, so without it the plant has no energy.
Nitrogen is a raw material that is combined with water to make glucose.
quiz.rationale: Nitrogen is a macronutrient used to build chlorophyll and proteins. Without it the leaves are pale, less light is trapped, photosynthesis is slower and growth is poor. Glucose is made from carbon dioxide and water, not nitrogen.
quiz.placement: Building the annotated model: section on at least two minerals and their deficiency

quiz.prompt: A smallholder farmer in Kiambu County finds that her kale leaves are pale and the plants grow slowly. They are grown in deep shade. Which action applies plant nutrition science best?
choices: Water the plants only at midday and keep them in deep shade, since shade stops all problems.
Spray the leaves with iodine solution to turn them green.
Move the plants to a spot with more sunlight and add manure or fertiliser that supplies nitrogen, so more chlorophyll and glucose are made.
Cover the plants with dark cloth to reduce photosynthesis and save glucose.
quiz.rationale: More light raises the rate of the light-dependent reactions, and nitrogen helps build chlorophyll. Together they increase photosynthesis and growth, which improves yield and food security. Deep shade fixes wilting but causes pallor and slow growth.
quiz.placement: Part 3 of the written task: The Kenyan Context (plant nutrition and food security)
